# A word about Glenmore

I had hoped to tell everyone about Glenmore myself, and instead some of you have heard about it from someone else. That is my fault. With the family spread between Boston and Perth and Leeds and everywhere else, I should have used this blog sooner. Úna set it up years ago so we could keep up with one another, and this is something you ought to have heard from me here, if I couldn’t tell you in person.

I have agreed a sale on the house. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it is due to close on **15 January 2027**. I am putting the date plainly at the beginning because I don’t want anyone getting another piece of this news second-hand.

The buyers are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house. It will be their home, not a holiday let.

I know that will not make the news easy for everyone. It hasn’t been easy for me either, though I realise I have had time to get used to the thought and some of you have had it landed on you without warning. I want to explain why I am selling, what we are keeping, and when we can all go out together before the house is cleared. I also want to say a few things that I should have said before now.

The old Mulkerrin place near Oughterard has been in the family since Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin, built it in 1931. That is a great deal of family life to have under one roof. Tom grew up there. For many of you it is a place you have known all your lives, and for some of the younger ones it is part of the Ireland you come home to. I understand that selling it changes something for more people than just me.

I have known that all along. Knowing it was part of what made it so difficult to begin the conversation, though that is an explanation and not an excuse for leaving it too late.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I have been driving out every fortnight to air the house and check the pipes. It is forty minutes each way. When I write that down, it doesn’t sound an enormous undertaking. There are plenty of people doing longer journeys every day, and I can hear myself making that argument because I have made it to myself often enough.

But the journey is only part of it. There is the worry between visits, and the jobs that need doing, and the knowledge that opening the windows for a while will not keep a house in repair. I kept thinking I could carry on a little longer and decide later. Over the best part of two years, I have come to realise that later would still leave me with the same decision.

The roof survey in September brought matters to a head. Ó Flaithearta’s found work needed on the slates and the back chimney, and the quote was €38,000. There is also the damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing to sell to anyone anyway.

I don’t give you those details to turn this into an account of expenses. You all know a house costs money, especially an old one. But I think you should know what keeping Glenmore actually means now. It is not simply a matter of leaving everything as it is and going out to put the heat on. There are substantial jobs to be done, and somebody has to take responsibility for getting them done.

I cannot go on being that person.

There is another thing I have not told you, and I expect some of you will be cross that you are only hearing it now. Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up.

I told nobody. I should have.

I don’t have a particularly good reason for keeping it to myself. I was able to get up in the end, and once I was home it was tempting to treat it as something that was over and didn’t need discussing. I also knew people would worry. That sounds foolish when I write it, because of course you would worry, and you would have been entitled to.

The truth is that I have been afraid of being alone at the house since then. I still go, and I still do what needs doing, but I am frightened of another fall. I am seventy-one. I don’t need to make myself helpless to admit that twenty minutes on the ground, with nobody knowing I was there, gave me a fright that has stayed with me.

I cannot keep making this decision on the basis of what I used to be comfortable doing. I am afraid there now, and I cannot go on maintaining it. Those are difficult things for me to say, but they are the truth.

When the Joyces made their offer, I thought seriously about what they wanted to do with the house. The price was fair. It was less than the Dublin crowd offered in the summer, and I accepted the lower offer on purpose.

I am not looking for praise for that. I had a choice, and I chose the people who wanted to make a home there. Aoife and Kevin have two small children, and it mattered to me that they intended to live in the house themselves.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I have thought about that often. I know I must be careful not to bring him into an argument as though he were here to settle it in my favour. He isn’t, and I miss being able to ask him what he thinks. But he did say it, and those of you who heard him will remember.

There is some comfort for me in the prospect of a family living there all year round. It does not take away the sadness of selling. I can be glad about who is buying it and still be very sorry to let it go.

I also need to say something about Declan.

He heard about the sale from his cousin Gráinne on a WhatsApp, not from me. He rang me at two in the morning his time. He was very upset, and he said I was “selling Dad”.

I said things back that I shouldn’t have said.

I am not going to put the rest of that conversation here. It was between the two of us, and writing this for everyone does not mean I should repeat every hurtful word. But I won’t leave it out altogether and give the impression that the news has been calmly received, or that I have been calm and sensible throughout. I haven’t.

Declan, I am sorry you found out that way. You should have heard from me. I regret not consulting you before I agreed the sale. I knew how much the place meant to you, and I should have given you the chance to speak to me about it before there was a decision to announce.

I am sorry for what I said on the phone as well.

I am not angry with you. I was hurt by what you said, but I know you were hurting too. You don’t have to agree with me before we can talk again. The door is open, and I hope you know that.

I do need to be honest about one thing: I am not willing to wait until your summer visit. The closing date is 15 January, and I intend to go ahead. I know that is not what you want to read. I would rather say it clearly than leave you thinking the decision is still waiting to be made.

I am sorry for how you found out, and for not speaking to you properly beforehand. I am not sorry for the decision itself. That may be hard to hear alongside an apology, but both are true.

There are things about Glenmore that I can hardly imagine belonging to somebody else. Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979, in the rain, with the cattle watching. It was hardly a grand romantic setting, though I wouldn’t exchange it for one. Of all the things that happened there, that is one I can still see very clearly.

Then there were the children learning to swim in the lake below the house. Declan, you would refuse to come out until your lips were blue. There was no persuading you that you were cold, even when the evidence was written all over your face.

I think of those days when I go out. Sometimes a memory is lovely company, and sometimes it makes the empty house harder to bear. I never quite know which it will be.

I don’t want to make Glenmore sound as though every day there was a happy one. It was a family house, with all that entails. But there was a great deal of happiness there, and ordinary life too, which is probably what I miss most. Tom belonged in that house in a way I can’t explain to anyone who didn’t see him there.

For a long time after he died, keeping it seemed like an obvious thing to do. I couldn’t have faced this decision then. Driving out and doing the small necessary jobs was something I could manage, and it let me put off the larger question.

I am ready to answer that question now, though ready is perhaps too cheerful a word for it. I have come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. It has taken me the best part of two years to believe that for myself. I wouldn’t expect everyone else to arrive at it just because I have written it here.

There are also things we are keeping, and I want everyone to know what they are.

The dresser is going to Úna’s. We are keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign. Those things are not going with the sale.

I know a list of belongings cannot answer every feeling people have about the place. Still, these are familiar things, and I hope it helps to know that they will remain with the family. I want to be clear about that now rather than have anyone wondering afterwards what became of them.

The Joyces have also said that family can come out and walk the land any time. I was very glad of that. We will, of course, remember that it will be their home, and give them the consideration we would want ourselves. But they understand that there is a family history there, and their willingness to welcome us matters to me.

It won’t be the same as having our own key. I know that. I am not going to pretend nothing will change.

Before it does, I would like us to have a day together at the house. **Sunday 13 December**, for anyone who can come, before it is cleared. There will be soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies.

I know December is awkward, especially for those of you abroad. Nobody is being asked to cross the world at short notice, and I don’t want anyone feeling guilty because they can’t get there. I would simply like those who can come to have the chance to spend some time in the house and walk outside together.

You can be sad about it. You can tell a story I have heard twenty times. You can disagree with me. I would only ask that we are kind to one another. There has been enough hurt already, some of it caused by my not saying things when I should have.

I would like to see the house full of us once more before it is cleared, but I don’t want to put too much weight on the day either. Soup, sandwiches, a walk if the weather allows, and time together. That will be enough.

For those who cannot come, I hope this post at least means you have the news properly, in my own words. The house was built by Pádraig Mulkerrin in 1931. It was Tom’s home, and it has been an important place for all of us. I have agreed to sell it to Aoife and Kevin Joyce, who want to raise their children there. The sale is due to close on **15 January 2027**.

I am sad about it, and I am relieved too. I have found the relief difficult to admit, as though it means I didn’t love the place enough. But I am tired of worrying about the house, and I will be glad not to be making those journeys alone. That doesn’t cancel out what it has meant to me.

I should have told you sooner. I should have spoken to Declan before agreeing the sale. I cannot put that right by explaining it well now, but I can at least stop leaving things unsaid.

You are all very welcome on 13 December. Declan, that includes you, if there is any way you can be there. And whether you can come or not, I would be glad to hear from you.
